questions.passage:
Few conventions are as thoroughly naturalised as the time on the clock. We tend to assume that noon is a fact about the sky, and that the hour shown at a railway station is merely a report of that fact. Yet for most of history noon was a local affair: each town set its clocks by the moment the sun stood highest overhead, and a traveller moving a few kilometres east or west found the local hour a little different from the last. The difference was irrelevant so long as news and people moved at the speed of a horse. In nineteenth-century Britain, clocks in Bristol ran about ten minutes behind those in London, and nobody thought this a scandal. The standardisation of time, which replaced thousands of such local times with a handful of regional ones, is therefore commonly told as a story of technical necessity: railways made journeys fast enough for the differences to matter, timetables were needed to run them safely, and timetables needed a common clock.

The story is not false, but it is incomplete in a way that is revealing. The railways did need coordination; what they did not need was any particular solution. A network can be coordinated on London time, on Bristol time or on a compromise between them, and trains will run equally safely under any of the three, so long as everyone uses the same one. Economists call this a coordination problem, and its defining feature is that the technical constraint establishes that a standard is required but not which standard. That question is settled by other considerations: who holds authority, whose convenience counts, and who bears the cost of adjustment. The Great Western Railway adopted London time across its lines in 1840, and other companies followed over the next decades; but it was not until 1880 that Parliament made Greenwich time the legal time of Britain, long after most of the work had been done by private firms.

The American experience was more dramatic. Across a continent, railways had accumulated dozens of local times, and large stations displayed a row of clocks, one for each company that used them. On 18 November 1883 the companies themselves imposed four time zones, without any legislation, and the day became known as the day of two noons because clocks in many cities had to be reset. Congress did not give the arrangement the force of law until 1918. Some cities, proud of their solar time, resisted for years, regarding the new hour as a surrender of local dignity to corporate convenience. The arrangement was practical, but it was not disinterested. Passengers and shippers gained from clarity; the railways gained more, since confusion over times produced accidents, missed connections and disputes over liability. That the beneficiary of a convention should also be its author is not unusual; it is, rather, a reason to ask whose interests a supposedly neutral standard serves.

The same pattern appears at the global level. In 1884 a conference in Washington voted overwhelmingly to adopt the meridian passing through Greenwich as the prime meridian, largely because most of the world's shipping already relied on charts drawn from it. France, which preferred its own Paris meridian, abstained, and continued to keep Paris time for years afterwards. The episode illustrates how standards are often settled by early adoption amplified by switching costs, rather than by any measurable superiority: once most ships used one meridian, the cost of moving to another exceeded any gain that its advocates could demonstrate. Standards, in this sense, resemble the layout of a keyboard: nobody would defend the arrangement on its merits, yet no individual typist can profitably defect from it. Path dependence, not design, explains the result.

Standardisation also changed how people lived. The historian E. P. Thompson argued that industrial capitalism taught workers to treat time as currency, to be spent rather than passed, and that the factory clock was an instrument of discipline. A population that can be synchronised can be scheduled; punctuality, once a courtesy, became a virtue and then a requirement, and lateness a failing of character. Yet it would be too simple to treat the clock merely as an employer's tool. Workers fought over the clock as well: the struggle for a shorter working day, a central demand of the labour movement, took the standard hour as common ground, and the slogan of eight hours presupposed that hours were uniform and countable.

Even physics felt the pressure. Historians of science have noted that Einstein, while working in the Swiss patent office, reviewed applications for devices that synchronised distant clocks, a practical problem that lay close to his theoretical interest in simultaneity. Whatever its causal role, the coincidence shows that synchrony, which now seems a given, was an engineering achievement long before it became a concept.

The politics of the clock has not disappeared. China, which spans five geographical zones, keeps a single time, and in its far west the sun rises late in the morning by the official clock. India adopted one national time over a more modest east-west span, but in Assam the tea gardens retained an hour-ahead garden time set by colonial planters to make better use of daylight, and the case for a separate north-eastern zone is periodically revived. In each instance a single time buys administrative unity and a symbol of national cohesion, at the price of a mismatch between the clock and the daylight, a mismatch that falls most heavily on those furthest from the chosen meridian.

The upshot is not that standard time is arbitrary, still less that it was imposed by conspiracy. Coordination has real benefits, and nobody seriously proposes a return to town time. It is that the clock encodes decisions, about whose convenience counts, which network advantages to ratify and how much local variation to tolerate, which, once made, present themselves as natural facts. What we regard as natural is often the residue of a settled argument whose terms we have forgotten.
questions.question: Which of the following best captures the central argument of the passage?
options: A) Standard time was an invention of railway companies pursuing profit, which shows that technical necessity played almost no part in its adoption.
B) The clock disciplined industrial workers into punctuality, and the history of time standardisation is therefore chiefly a history of labour control by employers.
C) Standard time answers a genuine need for coordination, yet which standard prevailed reflects power and convenience, later forgotten as natural.
D) Single national time zones such as those of China and India are irrational, because they ignore the differences in daylight across large countries.
questions.explanation: Explanation: The author accepts the technical story ('not false') but argues that necessity fixed only the need for some standard, while power, convenience and early adoption decided which. B overstates ('almost no part'); C and D take single strands (Thompson, China/India) as the whole thesis, and D adds a verdict the author never gives.

questions.question: The author's observation that the railways did not need "any particular solution" implies that
options: A) the need for a common standard, by itself, did not settle which standard would be adopted.
B) railway companies cared little whether their clocks were accurate.
C) the choice of Greenwich time was arbitrary, and had no lasting consequences for anyone affected by it afterwards.
D) Parliament's act of 1880 was unnecessary, because private firms had already settled the question completely by then.
questions.explanation: Explanation: A coordination problem needs a standard, but several candidates work equally well; so the technical constraint does not pick one. B misreads 'safely'; C says 'no consequences' and 'arbitrary', which go beyond the passage (the choice was settled by authority and convenience); D contradicts the point that legal force came later and still mattered.

questions.question: Which of the following is best supported by the passage's account of the 1884 conference?
options: A) Greenwich was chosen because its location made it scientifically superior to Paris for measuring longitude at sea.
B) France's abstention shows that the decisions of the conference carried no weight with any of the nations that had attended it.
C) The conference ended the practice of local time, since every country represented at it adopted Greenwich time at once.
D) Greenwich prevailed mainly because existing use made it costly to displace, not because it was demonstrably better.
questions.explanation: Explanation: The passage says shipping already relied on Greenwich charts and that switching costs exceeded any demonstrable gain of alternatives. B contradicts 'any measurable superiority'. C and D overgeneralise: only France is said to have held out, and local times persisted.

options: A) punctuality came to be regarded as a virtue

questions.question: Which of the following, if true, would most weaken the author's claim that the technical needs of the railways did not determine which standard was adopted?
options: A) Several countries adopted different standards at about the same time, each for reasons of national convenience.
B) Some towns, proud of their solar time, resisted the new standard for years after railways had adopted it.
C) Trains could be run safely only under one particular time, and every alternative risked collisions.
D) The costs of resetting clocks fell more heavily on small towns than on the large cities served by the railways.
questions.explanation: Explanation: The claim is that any shared time would have worked equally well. If safety required one particular time, technical need would determine the standard. B supports the claim, and C and D concern resistance and costs, not what the technical constraint required.

Workers fought over the clock as well: the struggle for a shorter working day, a central demand of the labour movement, took the standard hour as common ground, and the slogan of eight hours presupposed that hours were uniform and countable.

Even physics felt the pressure. Historians of science have noted that Einstein, while working in the Swiss patent office, reviewed applications for devices that synchronised distant clocks, a practical problem that lay close to his theoretical interest in simultaneity. Whatever its causal role, the coincidence shows that synchrony, which now seems a given, was an engineering achievement long before it became a concept.

The politics of the clock has not disappeared. China, which spans five geographical zones, keeps a single time, and in its far west the sun rises late in the morning by the official clock. India adopted one national time over a more modest east-west span, but in Assam the tea gardens retained an hour-ahead garden time set by colonial planters to make better use of daylight, and the case for a separate north-eastern zone is periodically revived. In each instance a single time buys administrative unity and a symbol of national cohesion, at the price of a mismatch between the clock and the daylight, a mismatch that falls most heavily on those furthest from the chosen meridian.

The upshot is not that standard time is arbitrary, still less that it was imposed by conspiracy. Coordination has real benefits, and nobody seriously proposes a return to town time. It is that the clock encodes decisions, about whose convenience counts, which network advantages to ratify and how much local variation to tolerate, which, once made, present themselves as natural facts. What we regard as natural is often the residue of a settled argument whose terms we have forgotten.
questions.question: The author's discussion of China and Assam implies that a single national time
options: A) buys administrative unity at the price of a daylight mismatch borne mainly by peripheral regions.
B) is always welfare-reducing, since no country should adopt one clock for a territory with a significant east-west extent.
C) was imposed in both countries by colonial administrators and has been resented by every region ever since.
D) has no effect on daily life, because people in distant regions simply ignore the official time and follow the sun.
questions.explanation: Explanation: The paragraph says a single time buys unity and symbolic cohesion at the cost of a mismatch falling on those furthest from the meridian. B ('always', 'no country should') is too strong; C is wrong for China and invents resentment; D overstates informal local timekeeping.

questions.question:
Choose the option that best completes the sentence:

The minister's speech was a masterpiece of ________, speaking at length without committing to a single position.
options: A) grandiloquence
B) equivocation
C) exhortation
D) candour
questions.explanation: Explanation: 'Equivocation' is deliberately ambiguous speech that avoids commitment. 'Grandiloquence' (pompous language) is tempting because the speech is long, but the sentence stresses non-commitment. 'Exhortation' urges action; 'candour' is the opposite of the behaviour described.

questions.question:
Choose the option that best completes the sentence:

Her ________ praise left the author wondering whether the review was a compliment at all.
options: A) wholehearted
B) unqualified
C) effusive
D) backhanded
questions.explanation: Explanation: A 'backhanded' compliment carries a hidden slight, which explains the author's doubt. 'Wholehearted', 'unqualified' and 'effusive' all describe generous praise that would raise no doubt.

questions.question:
Choose the option that best completes the sentence:

The treaty was dismissed as a dead letter, since ________.
options: A) it had been signed by more nations than any earlier agreement of its kind in the history of diplomacy
B) it was enforced so rigorously that no signatory dared to breach any of its provisions
C) no signatory either meant to honour it or could be made to
D) its provisions were too detailed to be summarised in a single sentence by the press
questions.explanation: Explanation: A dead letter is a rule that exists on paper but has no force. Only the first option explains that. B praises its reach, C describes strict enforcement, and D is irrelevant to whether it has force.

questions.question:
Choose the option that best fills the blanks:

The once-incisive columnist's recent essays were ________: they ________ the slogans of his youth without the argument that had once ________ them.
options: A) stale; rehearsed; underpinned
B) stale; repudiated; underpinned
C) stale; rehearsed; undermined
D) provocative; refined; contradicted
questions.explanation: Explanation: 'Stale' essays that 'rehearsed' (repeated) old slogans, minus the argument that once 'underpinned' (supported) them. B fails because he would not repudiate slogans while repeating them; C fails because an argument that undermined the slogans would not be missed; D contradicts the sense of decline.

questions.question:
Choose the option that best fills the blanks:

Though the diplomat's manner was ________, his demands were ________, and his hosts mistook the courtesy for ________.
options: A) urbane; negotiable; weakness
B) urbane; exacting; weakness
C) surly; modest; goodwill
D) abrupt; stringent; warmth
questions.explanation: Explanation: A courteous manner ('urbane') contrasts with severe demands ('exacting'), and the hosts wrongly read the courtesy as weakness. In B, 'negotiable' demands would make the mistake reasonable and kill the contrast; C and D describe a rude manner, which cannot be mistaken for courtesy.

questions.question:
Choose the best replacement for the portion in square brackets:

Hardly had the committee convened [than the chairman announced his resignation].
options: A) than had the chairman announced his resignation
B) then the chairman announced his resignation
C) before had the chairman announced his resignation
D) when the chairman announced his resignation
questions.explanation: Explanation: 'Hardly' (like 'scarcely') takes 'when', not 'than'; 'than' belongs with 'no sooner'. The other options mix constructions or invert the clause wrongly.

questions.question:
Choose the best replacement for the portion in square brackets:

The new curriculum aims at [improving analytical skills, to encourage independent reading, and developing] the capacity for sustained argument.
options: A) to improve analytical skills, encouraging independent reading, and developing
B) improving analytical skills, to encourage independent reading, and to develop
C) improving analytical skills, encouraging independent reading, and developing
D) the improvement of analytical skills, encouraging independent reading, and developing
questions.explanation: Explanation: After the preposition 'at' all items must be gerunds in parallel: improving, encouraging, developing. The other options mix infinitives, gerunds and noun phrases.

questions.question:
Complete the paragraph logically:

'It is tempting to suppose that a language with few speakers is a language in decline. ________ Icelandic, spoken by fewer than four hundred thousand people, is thriving, protected by a literary tradition, an institutional commitment to coining native words, and the pride of its speakers. Conversely, some languages with millions of speakers are losing the young, who find that the language of the market offers more.'
options: A) Small languages should therefore be allowed to disappear, since they cannot compete with languages that have many speakers.
B) Numbers alone, however, say little about vitality; what matters is whether the young are still learning the language.
C) Governments have rarely taken any interest in the survival of languages with few speakers, in any part of the world.
D) Icelandic is, in fact, the only small language in the world to have survived the pressures of globalisation intact.
questions.explanation: Explanation: The blank must challenge the 'tempting' assumption and set up both examples (a small thriving language, large ones losing the young). Only the first does. B endorses the assumption; C and D do not connect to the contrast that follows.

questions.question:
Complete the paragraph logically:

'When a hospital reports that its surgeons have a higher mortality rate than the national average, the natural inference is that they are less skilled. ________ A hospital that accepts the sickest patients, whom other hospitals turn away, will record more deaths even if its surgeons are the best in the country. The raw figure thus mixes the quality of care with the severity of the cases.'
options: A) The inference, however, is unsafe, because the rate depends on who is treated as well as on how they are treated.
B) The inference is sound, since mortality is the only reliable measure of how skilled a surgeon actually is.
C) Hospitals therefore have no reason to publish mortality figures, since patients do not understand statistics and may be misled.
D) National averages are computed by the government, and are for that reason unreliable as a standard of comparison.
questions.explanation: Explanation: The sentences that follow explain why the natural inference fails: case mix. B endorses the inference; C and D introduce unrelated claims.

questions.question: One of the statements below contains a word used incorrectly or inappropriately. Choose the option which has the incorrect or inappropriate usage of the word.
options: A) The council decided to censure the official for misusing public funds entrusted to the department.
B) The theory was widely regarded as credible, given the weight of the evidence assembled in its support.
C) The new policy is expected to alleviate the shortage of skilled workers in the manufacturing sector.
D) She is not adverse to taking risks, provided the rewards are large enough.
questions.explanation: Explanation: 'Adverse' means harmful or unfavourable; the sentence needs 'averse' (opposed). 'Censure' (criticise formally), 'credible' (believable) and 'alleviate' (ease) are used correctly.

questions.question: One of the statements below contains a word used incorrectly or inappropriately. Choose the option which has the incorrect or inappropriate usage of the word.
options: A) The doctor will prescribe a course of antibiotics for the infection once the test results arrive.
B) The firm was fined for engaging in elicit trade in protected timber, which it had carried on for years.
C) Historians often ascribe the collapse of the empire to financial exhaustion rather than to defeat in war.
D) The principal reason for the delay was a shortage of funds, which the board had failed to anticipate.
questions.explanation: Explanation: Trade that is against the law is 'illicit'; 'elicit' means to draw out. 'Prescribe', 'ascribe' and 'principal' are all correct in their sentences.

questions.question:
Rearrange the four sentences (1-4) into a logical sequence (Type the 4-digit sequence as answer):

1. Even so, the legend has endured because it offers a tidy moral about the folly of crowds.
2. Recent historians, however, have questioned how large the episode really was.
3. The Dutch tulip mania of the 1630s is often cited as the archetypal speculative bubble.
4. Their research suggests that few people were ruined by the price collapse, and that stories of fortunes lost over a single bulb owe more to pamphleteers than to court records.
questions.explanation: Explanation: 3 introduces the tulip mania as the archetypal bubble. 2 ('however') begins to challenge it. 4 ('Their research') continues with those historians' findings. 1 ('Even so, the legend') explains why the story persisted despite them. Order: 3-2-4-1.

questions.passage:
Interviewer: Professor, Punjab pumps out more groundwater than the rains replace. Why don't farmers simply grow less water-hungry crops?

Professor: Because from the farmer's seat the decision is perfectly rational. Paddy is the crop with an assured purchase at a known price, and the power for the pump is nearly free. The water is the one input whose price is zero, and nobody economises on what costs nothing. Add to that the fact that the aquifer is shared: if I save a litre, it only benefits the neighbour who pumps it instead.

Interviewer: So it's a tragedy of the commons?

Professor: Partly. But I would caution against using the phrase as a full explanation, because commons have been managed sustainably for centuries wherever users could watch one another and punish defectors. The commons part of the problem would be soluble. What makes Punjab hard is that the state has, in effect, subsidised the overuse, and that part is politics.

Interviewer: Then why not price the electricity?

Professor: Because the farmers are voters, and every government that has tried has retreated. The alternative I find more promising is to pay farmers to leave water in the ground: a payment per hectare for switching crops, funded from the savings on the subsidy. That makes the sensible choice also the profitable one.
questions.question: According to the professor, groundwater is overused in Punjab chiefly because
options: A) farmers are unaware that the water table is falling and have never been told how much water they pump.
B) paddy is the only crop that can be grown profitably in the region, whatever the price of water or electricity.
C) each farmer's incentives, including free power and an assured market for paddy, reward heavy pumping.
D) the aquifer is privately owned by the largest farmers, who sell the water to their neighbours at inflated prices.
questions.explanation: Explanation: He says the decision is 'perfectly rational' for the farmer: assured purchase, free power, zero-priced water, and a shared aquifer. B is not his argument (his point is about incentives, though he says nobody can see the table); C and D invent claims.

questions.question: The professor's reservation about the phrase "tragedy of the commons" implies that
options: A) commons problems can be solved where users monitor one another, so the subsidy is the harder obstacle.
B) Punjab's aquifer is not a commons at all, since no farmer has any right to draw water from it.
C) the subsidy on electricity should be kept, because commons can be managed only through generous state support.
D) the overuse of groundwater is inevitable, since commons have never been managed sustainably by their users.
questions.explanation: Explanation: He says commons have been managed sustainably where users can watch and punish defectors, and that the subsidy is 'the politics'. B contradicts his statement that the aquifer is shared; C and D reverse his argument.
